title: Compassion, Part 1: All Beings Want Happiness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Tibetan contemplation that all beings want happiness and freedom from suffering, then turns to Gateless Gate case 16, where Yunmen asks why monastics put on the seven-piece robe at the sound of the bell when the world is so vast and wide. Nomon tells of the family cat Luca dying, of a head full of platitudes giving way to shared sorrow with Janet, and of Janet then objecting that Nomon and Janet's son had planned the weekend as if she didn't exist. Muman's verse, in which all things are one family and disconnected both with and without realization, leads Nomon to ask how to answer the bell after the bombings in Belgium. Nomon closes with the Dhammapada lines on hate being conquered by love.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
I was just thinking, for us it seems to be so important to say the right thing.
We always want to say the right thing, and have some kind of exchange of concepts that are mediated by sounds that we call words, all this complicated thing we do.
That's so important to us, and it is, as well it should be.
But I was thinking before we started, what if it was just as important to us, just as valuable to us, to recognize our breathing the same air, when we're just sharing the same space?
Why is that any less important, or less valuable?
And then if you have to give the talk you can relax a little bit, because we're breathing the same air, it doesn't matter what I say.
Anyway, I expected to be giving this talk a week ago, and for me it feels like so much has happened in the last week.
Maybe you feel that way too.
It doesn't seem like a lot has happened in the last week, and probably a lot has always happened in the last week.
There may just be weeks that we didn't notice it as much, which in some ways is what we desire, it seems like.
We like to be a little checked out, not too much going on, everything's cool.

When I was sitting writing this talk, our little cat Luca, a little black cat, of course we thought she was the smartest, most engaging cat, really a friend, a dear friend and family member in the household, seemed to be doing poorly.
We didn't know how poorly.
She wasn't moving around too much anymore.
She'd always been very sprightly, very cheerful, and she liked to play fetch, like dogs do.
Some cats do that, they'll play fetch, and she had been doing that not that long ago, before last week.
Anyway, in the afternoon it seemed like she was moving less and less, and then at about six o'clock we had the mobile vet come over.
If you ever have animals you should know about the mobile vet, this is a really good thing.
They'll just come to your house, and it doesn't really cost any more than going to the vet that's in the building.
This little cat was especially dear to my wife, and I was noticing Janet kind of going in and out of some idea of accepting that she was dying.
Maybe there were only a few more days or a few more hours, we didn't know, or maybe if we had a little more information or some medication or something, maybe another week or two.
I could feel myself kind of riding those waves of speculation with her: who knows, we don't really know what's coming.
But anyway, at about six o'clock last Wednesday, I had the talk already written, I was expecting to come here, the vet came in, and she took one look at the cat.
You could just tell instantly that the vet knew, and was going to try to figure out how to very kindly tell us that it was more like a couple of hours than a couple of days.
So it was interesting to feel myself shifting gears to this new reality.
This is always what we're doing, right?
The reality is always shifting.
We think it's one way or this way or that way, and then suddenly the reality is a different way.
The other day, when I was thinking about this talk, I had an interesting kind of sense during my morning zazen practice, a feeling of vividness and connectedness and aliveness.
Of course, I don't have this subjective experience all the time during meditation, and don't feel bad if you don't always feel vividly alive and alert during zazen.
Somehow zazen continues to function and support our life, no matter what our subjective experience is, whether we feel vivid and alive or half asleep or grumpy and annoyed by the whole thing.
But it's nice when we feel vivid and alive.
What came into my mind was a thought from the Tibetan teachings on compassion.
The Tibetan system involves studying profound thoughts and teachings and really turning them over in your mind and contemplating them.
I don't know a lot about it, but a little bit.
The central thought in the study of compassion is that all beings want happiness and freedom from suffering.
All beings without exception want happiness and freedom from suffering.
Somehow this popped into my mind that morning, and I don't know how to describe it, but it just felt like, well, then it's okay.
When somebody's difficult with me, the people in my life that I find difficult, here's a being that wants happiness and freedom from suffering.
A beautiful being, no matter what her or his manifestation, is an expression of the desire for happiness and joy and the challenge of suffering.

The idea is that if we contemplate this deeply over many years, maybe many lifetimes in that system, we'll understand that it makes no sense to ever be annoyed with anybody, to ever feel anything but compassion and love and connection.
Even for people who are actively harming us or being in some direct way difficult for us.
"All beings want happiness and freedom from suffering" reminds us to look around and notice the true nature of everyone around us, including ourselves.

And when we're facing death, whether it's a beautiful little cat, or [unclear: "there are noticed"] right now on the Manjushri altar, there are many names, presumably of human people who have died, when we're facing death, it makes it a little easier to remember how important these studies are.
Although we get busy and have a lot of important things to do and think about, we can also recognize that we're all in the vast waiting room, waiting for death.
And we try to forget that death's just behind that door.
Someone's just telling me that they had a dream visualizing the clothing of death, the black cowl.

This thought, all beings want happiness and freedom from suffering, can help us to look around in this big waiting room and see that the people who are distracting themselves on their cell phones in the waiting room of death, and the people who are trying to straighten their furniture and clean up, and the people who are trying to take care of other people, sometimes skillfully, sometimes not so skillfully, they all want happiness.
They all want freedom from suffering.
The word compassion requires some feeling like this.
The passion in that word means passionate, feeling something deeply.

There's no actual compassion without not only recognizing that people want happiness and freedom from suffering, but recognizing and feeling directly in our own bodies that in fact that suffering is really present, that it's really there.
The Buddha talked about three broad categories of suffering, and all three of these are always functioning.
There's the obvious category of things that are directly painful and difficult, that we can notice directly in our consciousness: ouch, I don't like that.
Then a little more subtle category of suffering: change is so difficult for us.
This beautiful cat who lived in our house for 17 years, it's difficult to accept the change of her not being there.
This is suffering.
And the third level of suffering is kind of a pervasive sense, a subtle and pervasive sense of something's not quite right, a sense of dis-ease.
Recently, what I realized is we often have in the back of our mind some quality, some feeling, some half-formed thought.
It's kind of like, there's something wrong.
Do you have this feeling?
There's something wrong.
You can't quite put your finger on it necessarily, but there's something wrong here.
So this is the subtle quality of suffering that the Buddha talked about, that we're all working with, we're all practicing with all the time.
I noticed when we started recognizing that this little cat, Luca, was beginning to decline, that my wife was directly upset.
She was a little teary, a little tight, that kind of tightness in the gut.
And I wasn't really feeling that much.
I was sympathetic.
I had the thought in my mind, oh, this is too bad, this is not good.
But it was really more in my head.
My head was kind of going to platitudes that I was trying not to say to my wife.
Like, oh, it's okay, she's had a long life.
Or, of course, this is inevitable.
It doesn't help anybody to say these things.
Or, if she won't have a high quality of life, we should just let her go.
If you say these things without feeling something, it just is harmful.
You don't say these things, even though they're true.

But I noticed little by little, I was starting to feel a little more the pain of this, and the sadness of loving and losing that had manifested itself in the form of a little eight pound black fuzzy creature.
Little by little, I started feeling this.
And then suddenly I could be with my wife in a much more helpful way.
We could be together in our sorrow, instead of me standing on the outside trying to help her out or cheer her up.
We could feel together that we want freedom from suffering, and this requires feeling the suffering.
So then the funny thing was, I was sitting there on the couch actually writing this talk and feeling good about figuring that out.
Feeling the suffering a little more, that's good, that can be a little more compassionate, which is good.
It's good when you notice these things.
And I don't know how it came up, but I know what it was.
The morning before, at breakfast, my son and I always have breakfast together.
It's one of the times I reliably see him during the day.
He knew that the upcoming weekend, this last weekend, I was home, which unfortunately is a little rarer than it should be.
So we were eagerly making plans.
We planned out the whole weekend, which games we were going to play and all the things we were going to do.
And Janet was upstairs, I assumed asleep.
I don't really think about it.
She has some energy issues, so she's often still in bed when we're having breakfast.

So anyway, at this moment that I had just written these lines and was feeling good about being a compassionate human being and able to share the suffering of this cat with her, she turns to me and says, it really upset me, the way you and Walker were talking about the weekend as if I didn't exist.
She went on and told me why that wasn't okay with her, which I could agree with.
And then she had several other examples of similar behavior on my part.
And then that feeling of sympathy went away, and I noticed anger arising.
I listened, tried to say something to verify for her that I'd actually heard what she said, and then she left.
Then I realized, well, there's a lot of layers to this.
There's a lot of layers to compassion and to the deep thought that all beings want happiness.
They want to be loved.
They want to be honored.
They want to be included in your weekend plans.
They want to be recognized.
They want happiness.
They want freedom from suffering.
And then I could sit there and practice with that and sink into that and feel into that.

So it's an endless process, this being human, breathing the same air with other beings, cat beings, human beings, all kinds of beings, recognizing that we so easily become disconnected and abstract, self-focused, and project our limited views, and other beings forget that they want happiness and freedom from suffering.
It helps us to have practice and teachings to remind us.
Lately I've really been enjoying studying a set of those teachings in the Zen koan literature, which in its quirky way is about this exact same topic.
A group of us have been studying the stories in one of the major collections of Zen koans, pithy little Zen stories.
I wanted to share with you a wonderful story in that collection, called the Gateless Gate collection, case 16.
The story is this:
*Yunmen said, see how vast and wide the world is.
Why do you put on your seven piece robe at the sound of the bell?*
That's the entire story.
They're short mostly, very short.
*Yunmen said, see how vast and wide this world is.

Why do you put on your seven piece robe at the sound of the bell?* Yunmen was an important Zen teacher in a period of China that most of these stories are about, the Tang and early Song dynasty, 10th to 12th century more or less.
So the teacher is asking us a question.
Something about the world, something about responding to the world.
The seven piece robe is this garment that monastics wear, and presumably his audience were a group of monastics wearing this robe.
Putting it on means going to practice, going to the Zen hall to practice.
So the world is vast and wide, right?
Full of beings trying to be happy, trying to work with suffering.
So why is this the right response, to put on the robe, to go to practice at the sound of the bell?
How do we respond to the calls of the world?
And what a world it is.
As he says, vast and wide.
He wasn't getting instant updates on Facebook, right?
But even with our constant instant updates about all the things that are happening, of course we don't know the whole of it, do we?
Receiving lots of information about a very narrow slice of what's happening, and from there we create a world in our minds.
But surely it's vaster and wider than that, fuller than that.
So how do we meet this world?

When our beloved animals and our friends and our family all die, and we actually remember that they are all dying, every single one without exception, and people we don't know, blown up in Belgium and Ankara and Baghdad and everywhere else, how can we meet this world?
It's so interesting the way it's easier to feel the pain of the world when you get up at two in the morning and the cat is no longer a cat somehow.
It's a black furry shape still, but the posture and the feeling and the energy of this object in the world is so different.
It's easier to feel the suffering of the world then than when we hear the news.
But two weeks ago, 35 families in Belgium were going about their business doing whatever they were doing.
And then one week ago, 35 families were in mourning, and the bell rings.
Do we put on the seven panel robe and go to practice?
Are we angry at being reminded of our limited views?
Are we despairing and defeated?
Is there any point to anything?
Should one in the waiting room of death simply wait because there's nothing you can do?
Or are there people to love and children to feed?
The collector of this particular set of stories added commentaries and verses to each story, which sometimes help us to make sense of it.
Sometimes they're just baffling.
In this case, he reminds us that we true Zen students can access a bigger view, a view that's wider than any view.
He says in the comments to this case, I'm supposed to read you the comments.
Not only did I write this a week ago, but I don't have my glasses.
Excuse me one more.
Maybe a little more light would be good.
Can I have a little more light, if there is more available?
Because I didn't set that up and now I'm paying off.
It's like a bad movie.
Well, let's just skip that part.
But I do have his verse.
He writes a commentary in a verse.
Muman or Wuman was his name.
The verse starts out in an interesting way that makes sense.
The verse starts out with realization:
*With realization, all things are one family.
With realization, all things are one family.*
So if we realize something deep about this thought, live this thought, all beings want happiness and freedom from suffering, we realize in a fundamental way that all things are one family.
And then he goes on:
*Without realization, all things are disconnected.*
I'm here, you are there.
It's not my problem.
It's far away.
We're disconnected.
So that makes sense.
But then, a little bit like we've heard from our dear Zen Master Dogen, he turns it around, because reality is never so one-sided as that.
Then he says:
*Without realization, all things are one family.
With realization, all things are disconnected.*
So it's very interesting.
*With realization, all things are one family.
Without realization, all things are disconnected.
Without realization, all things are one family.
With realization, all things are disconnected.* Are there things after all, anyway, that can be connected and disconnected?
That can be family and non-family?
When the world calls and we respond, are we over here on the couch, feeling a little smug in our compassion practice?
Or are we already with our dear ones?
Can we feel the world fully, suffering and joy, and respond fully?
Or do we bury our nose in the magazines in the waiting room and keep busy with our tasks?
All this makes me think of the name that Norman Fischer gave me.
When we give and receive names in our tradition, the names are supposed to both honor equality in the person and then remind them that you're never quite done.
So the name he gave me means responding gate.
Sometimes it seems like our gates swing freely and all beings pass easily into the garden.
Other times the gate is sticky, rusty, creaking.
It doesn't want to open.
And I want to hide, and the I wants to hide.
So how is it for you when the bell rings, when you recognize and remember in some way the vastness of the world, and what kind of world are we creating?
Somebody sent me a few lines from the Dhammapada.
We'll close with this.
*What we are today comes from our thoughts of yesterday, and our present thoughts build our life of tomorrow.
Our life is the creation of our mind.
The person speaks or acts with an impure mind.
Suffering follows as the wheel of the cart follows the beast that pulls it.
What we are today comes from our thoughts of yesterday and our present thoughts build our life of tomorrow.
The person speaks or acts with the pure mind.
Joy follows as the shadow follows the body.
He insulted me.
He hurt me.
He defeated me.
He robbed me.
Those who think such thoughts will not be free from hate.
For hate is not conquered by hate.
Hate is conquered by love.
This is the eternal law.*
So it might be this world is not outside, but this world is being created by all of us all the time.
*Our world today comes from our thoughts of yesterday.
Our present thoughts build our world of tomorrow.
Our world is the creation of our mind.
The person speaks or acts with impure mind.
Suffering follows as the wheel of the cart follows the beast that pulls.
What we all are today comes from our thoughts of yesterday and our present thoughts build our world of tomorrow.
If a person speaks or acts with the pure mind, a joyful world follows as a shadow follows the body.
She insulted me.
He hurt me.
He defeated me.
She robbed me.
Those who think such thoughts will not be free.
Will not be free from hate.
For hate is not conquered by hate.
Hate is conquered by love.
This is the eternal law.*
Anyway, I hope that was in some way interesting or helpful.
That doesn't matter.
It's worth thinking about this thought as you go around your life.
It really is.
And it's so simple.
It's like, well, why would you have to think about that?
Everyone knows that.
It's so simple: all beings want happiness and freedom from suffering.
But what if we really lived in a way that really was an expression of understanding this?
What can we do but love?
Even when beings blow up airports, what can we do but love?
